title: JavaScript and the V8 engine
idea: JavaScript is a language. An engine such as V8 runs it. A runtime such as Node.js or a browser wraps an engine and adds what the language lacks.

analogy.text: A car engine only turns fuel into motion. Wheels, pedals and a dashboard connect it to the road and the driver. The runtime is the whole car.
analogy.breaks: One engine fits many cars: Chrome and Node.js both use V8.

points: The ECMAScript standard defines the language, so different engines run the same code.
V8 compiles your code as it runs, optimizing the busy parts.
File access (`fs`) and page access (`document`) come from runtimes, not from ECMAScript.
Node.js wraps V8 with file and network features, so JavaScript runs on servers.

steps.caption: Your source goes to V8. It parses and compiles the code, then runs the language: variables, loops, `Array`, `Promise`.
Node.js adds `fs`, `http` and `process` around V8. Now your code can read files and listen for requests.
A browser adds `document` and `window` instead. Chrome uses V8; Firefox and Safari use other engines.
Both runtimes reach the disk and network through the operating system. The language itself never does.

code.title: Language or runtime?
code.caption: Run it. In a browser tab, `document` would be an object and `process` would be `undefined`.

pitfalls: Do not use `window` or `document` in Node.js code: only browsers provide them.
Check your Node.js version before using new language features; older engines lack them.

quiz.q: In Node.js, what does this print?
quiz.why: `Promise` is part of the language, so every modern engine has it. `document` belongs to browsers; Node.js does not provide it.

takeaway: Same engine, different runtime: check where a feature comes from.
